subject: english-literature
title: Formalism and Marxism
welcome_lead: Two opposing lenses: one polishes the text in isolation, the other reads it as ideology's child.
meta_desc: Formalism and Marxist criticism at A-Level English Literature.
final_note: You have set form against ideology — and seen that the best readings often borrow from both.

concepts.def: Critical approach (Russian Formalists, New Criticism) focused on the autonomous text — form, image, ambiguity.
Shklovsky's term — art renews perception by making the familiar strange (ostranenie).
Anglo-American formalism (Brooks, Wimsatt) advocating close reading and the intentional fallacy.
Approach reading literature as shaped by class, ideology and economic base (Eagleton, Williams).
Marx's model — economic base shapes the cultural superstructure (art, law, religion).
Althusser — the imaginary relation of subjects to their real conditions of existence, reproduced in texts.

walkthroughs.body_html:
New Critics insisted on the autonomy of the text. Wimsatt and Beardsley's intentional fallacy (1946) bars author biography; the affective fallacy bars reader response.

What remains is the verbal artefact, prized for ambiguity, paradox and irony.
Russian Formalist Viktor Shklovsky argued art's purpose is ostranenie: making the stone stony again, refreshing perception dulled by habit.

Marxist criticism reads texts as both reflections and producers of ideology. Eagleton's Literary Theory (1983) is the great introduction.

A novel of bourgeois marriage reproduces a bourgeois ideology of selfhood — or, occasionally, ruptures it.
